Saddled
SAD-ld
v. (past t. and past part.)
From saddle, Saxon sadel. Webster 1828: covered with a saddle; furnished with a saddle. In Scripture the word marks the moment a man sets out, and it is used at two of the most consequential departures in the Old Testament.

Biblical Definition

Saddled is a small word that Scripture places at the head of great journeys. The greatest is Abraham’s: And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him (Genesis 22:3). Seven verbs in one verse, and not one word of protest, argument, or explanation — a man who had waited twenty-five years for the son now cutting the wood to burn him. The narrative gives us his obedience and withholds his thoughts, and Hebrews 11:19 supplies what he was reasoning: that God was able to raise Isaac from the dead. The word marks another early rising with the opposite spirit: And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with the princes of Moab (Numbers 22:21) — a prophet setting out on an errand God had permitted rather than commanded, and God’s anger was kindled because he went. And it marks the errand of the old prophet who went after the man of God and lied to him: And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass: and he rode thereon (1 Kings 13:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SADDLED as covered with a saddle; furnished with a saddle; and figuratively, loaded or burdened with something to be borne.

expand to see more

SADDLED, pp. — Covered or furnished with a saddle, as a beast for riding.

Loaded; burdened; as, saddled with a debt or an encumbrance.

SADDLE, n. — A seat to be placed on a horse’s or an ass’s back for the rider.

SADDLE, v.t. — To put a saddle on; and hence, to fix a burden or charge upon.

From Saxon sadel — connected with sit and with the Latin sedeo, to sit.

Key Scripture

Genesis 22:3 — "And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and clave the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him."

Numbers 22:21 — "And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with the princes of Moab."

1 Kings 13:13 — "And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass: and he rode thereon,"

2 Samuel 19:26 — "And he answered, My lord, O king, my servant deceived me: for thy servant said, I will saddle me an ass, that I may ride thereon, and go to the king; because thy servant is lame."

Modern Corruption

Genesis 22 is regularly softened into a story about a test God never intended to complete, or condemned outright as divine cruelty, and both readings avoid what the New Testament says the chapter is for.

expand to see more

The account is not offered as a general model for how God deals with fathers and sons; it is a single, unrepeatable command, given to the man through whom the promised seed was to come, and it is stopped by God Himself. Hebrews 11:17-19 tells us what was in Abraham’s mind: he accounted that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead, having been told that in Isaac shall thy seed be called. So Abraham reasoned from the promise, not against it. And the chapter’s deepest purpose is typological: a father and an only son, a three-day journey, wood carried by the son up the hill, the son asking where the lamb is, the answer God will provide himself a lamb, a substitute caught in a thicket, and a place named Jehovah-jireh on the mountain where the temple would later stand. What God did not require of Abraham He did not spare Himself: He that spared not his own Son (Romans 8:32).

Numbers 22:21 is the necessary counterweight. Balaam also rose early and saddled his ass, and God’s anger was kindled because he went — although God had said go with them. The distinction is between a permission wrung out of God by a man who kept asking, and a command. Balaam had already been told plainly, Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed, and he asked again. Scripture treats a permission obtained by persistence as a dangerous thing to hold, and Psalm 106:15 describes the same pattern in Israel: he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chabash (H2280), to bind on, to saddle, to bind up a wound; merkab (H4817), a saddle, a chariot seat; Greek epibaino (G1910), to mount, to go aboard.

expand to see more

Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind on, to gird; used both of saddling a beast and of binding up the brokenhearted (Isaiah 61:1).

Hebrew merkab (H4817) — a saddle or seat for riding; whatsoever saddle he rideth upon (Leviticus 15:9).

Hebrew athon (H860) — a she-ass; the beast Abraham and Balaam both saddled.

Greek epibaino (G1910) — to mount, to embark; used of Christ riding into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5).

Hebrew shakam (H7925) — to rise early; the verb that opens both Genesis 22:3 and Numbers 22:21.

Usage

"Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his ass (Genesis 22:3) — seven verbs of obedience, and no protest recorded."

"Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass (Numbers 22:21) — the same early rising on a permitted errand, and God’s anger kindled."

"Saddle me the ass. So they saddled him the ass (1 Kings 13:13) — an old prophet setting out to lie to a younger one."
